title: Conversion: portfolio matrices & conjoint analysis
source: Session 7 handout (DDM 26/27) – Lilien et al. (2017), Rao (2014) Applied Conjoint Analysis, Cooper (1993), pizza example, ESCP water bottle exercise, Polkaly & Ralph mock cases
tagline: To convert interest into purchases, a firm must offer the right products. Portfolio matrices (BCG, GE/McKinsey) decide which offerings to grow or drop; conjoint analysis finds the feature combination customers value most – and predicts what they would choose.
goals: explain why firms review their **portfolio** (product lines, SBUs)
place offerings in the **BCG** and **GE/McKinsey** matrices
use conjoint vocabulary: **attribute, level, profile, part-worth, relative importance**
compute **total utility**, the **best profile** and **relative importance** from part-worths
simulate **market shares** with a choice rule and judge a **price increase**

sections.heading: Why review the offering?
sections.lead: Johnson & Johnson sells baby shampoo to parents and knee prostheses to surgeons. Nobody can manage hundreds of products one by one – and optimising each product alone misses company goals.

steps.label: Products
steps.text: e.g. Neutrogena face wash, Aveeno face wash

steps.label: Strategic Business Units (SBUs)
steps.text: Lines of business targeting a common set of customers

sides.label: Benefits of a timely review
points: Maximise product investments and align them with business objectives
Identify strong and weak products to clarify resource allocation

sides.label: Goals of the amendments
points: Find products with high demand in growing markets
Allocate resources to promising innovations; improve or re-brand products in promising markets
Balance long- vs. short-term goals; link to corporate strategy

blocks.title: BCG growth–share matrix

cells.label: Question marks
cells.text: Growing market, weak position – invest heavily or divest

cells.label: Stars
cells.text: Leader in a growing market – invest to keep the lead

cells.label: Dogs
cells.text: Weak position in a slow market – harvest or drop

cells.label: Cash cows
cells.text: Dominates a slow-growth market – milk cash to fund stars and question marks

blocks.note: Polkaly mock case: the public sector (50 % size, 1 % growth) behaves like a cash cow; education (15 %, 3 %) is the question to be justified with more data.

sides.label: BCG matrix
points: X–Y graph of a product against its market
Two dimensions: market growth × relative market share
Four types: stars, cash cows, dogs, question marks

sides.label: GE/McKinsey matrix
points: Expanded BCG for diverse product families and acquisitions
Low–medium–high ratings (3×3) → develop, expand, re-tool or eliminate (same logic as targeting in S5)

blocks.text: To review and revise offerings, firms use the two NPD methods also for existing products: **A/B testing** (S6) compares two versions; **conjoint analysis** (this session) compares many feature combinations at once.

sections.heading: Conjoint analysis: idea and vocabulary
sections.lead: Products with a clearly defined offer are 3.3× as likely to succeed and earn higher share and profit (Cooper, 1993). Conjoint sharpens the definition by decomposing preferences for whole product bundles into the value of each attribute level.

items.text: A product feature being evaluated – laptop: brand, size, colour, battery life.
The specification of an attribute – brand: Samsung, Dell, Apple, Asus.
A hypothetical offering = one level per attribute.
How many times a respondent has to choose or rate.
The contribution of one attribute level to the total perceived value – e.g. Samsung −0.11, Dell 0.10, Apple 0.17, Asus −0.16.
How much total value changes when you move from the worst to the best level of an attribute, relative to all attributes (e.g. brand 35 %, price 30 %).

blocks.name: Additive conjoint model
vars: y_{k} = total perceived value of option k
β_{jm} = part-worth of level m of attribute j
x_{jm} = 1 if option k has that level, else 0
blocks.note: In mock cases a **baseline (intercept)** is added and the reference level of each attribute is set to 0.

blocks.name: Relative importance of an attribute
blocks.formula: Importance_{j} = range_{j} / Σ ranges     with range_{j} = max part-worth − min part-worth
blocks.note: Remember the reference level 0 when taking max and min – with levels 0, −1.22, −2.24 the range is 2.24.

sections.lead: Crust (3) × topping (4) × cheese type (3) × cheese amount (3) × price (3) = 324 possible pizzas, 16 levels to estimate – nobody tastes 324 pizzas, so a reduced set is tested.

blocks.caption: Pepperoni beats veggie by 20 points – exactly as much as paying $8.99 instead of $9.99. Topping is worth twice as much as crust. Preferences are individual: each customer has their own part-worths.

sections.heading: Exam cases: Polkaly, Ralph and the ESCP bottle

blocks.title: Polkaly – best combination for the education segment
blocks.question: Best profile, total utility and most important attribute?
steps: Pick the highest part-worth per attribute: in-window (1.24), unlimited (2.94), 100 participants (1.59), price 30 (0)
Ranges: chat 1.24 · groups 2.94 · participants 1.59 · price 2.71 → sum 8.48
blocks.result: Education: in-window chat, unlimited groups, 100 participants, price 30 → 9.95; breakout groups are the most important feature – and Polkaly's competitive advantage.

blocks.title: ESCP water bottle – the full conjoint workflow

steps.label: Attributes & levels
steps.text: Material (steel, copper, plastic) · size (250/500/1000 ml) · straw (yes/no) · price (12/20/25 €)

steps.label: Best option & importance
steps.text: Per respondent: highest-value profile; ranges → relative importance

steps.label: Market simulation
steps.text: Each respondent buys the option with the highest value (first choice) – variant: only if value > 4 (scale mean)

steps.label: Pricing
steps.text: Raise the favourite's price 10 %: still preferred over the 2nd option? Max WTP = price at which it stops being first choice

recap: Products → product lines → SBUs; review the portfolio to allocate resources and drop underperformers.
**BCG**: growth × relative share → stars, cash cows, question marks, dogs. **GE/McKinsey**: attractiveness × strength, 3×3.
Conjoint decomposes preferences for bundles into **part-worths** per attribute level.
Total utility = baseline + Σ part-worths of the chosen levels; best profile = best level of every attribute.
**Relative importance = range / sum of ranges** (include the 0 reference level).
Number of profiles = product of the numbers of levels (pizza 324, bottle 54).
Market share simulation: each respondent picks the highest-utility option (optionally above a threshold).
exam: Mini case with a part-worth table (Polkaly, Ralph): best combination per segment, total utility of a given product, most important attribute, effect of a price change.
T/F: reading single part-worths (“price 70 instead of 30 reduces utility by 2.24”).
Portfolio interpretation of a segment table (size vs. growth).
traps: The most important attribute is the one with the largest **range**, not the largest single part-worth.
Don't forget the **baseline/intercept** when computing total utility.
Negative part-worths are relative to the reference level, not absolute dislikes.
A higher price level can have a smaller utility loss (luxury signal) – read the table, don't assume.
